brief.situation: 03:05 on a medical-surgical unit. Mr. Ferraro, 81, is found sitting on the floor by his bed. He was trying to reach the bathroom without his walker, slipped and hit his forehead on the bedside table. He says he's fine and wants to go back to bed.
handover: Admitted with pneumonia. Atrial fibrillation on an oral anticoagulant (last dose 21:00). Bed alarm was off; walker across the room; the floor wet near the sink.

Hospital post-fall policy: don't move the patient until checked for injury; neurological observations every 30 minutes; the provider told of every fall, and called at once for a head strike on an anticoagulant with any drop in level of consciousness, vomiting or worsening headache, for an urgent CT.
The night provider is in the hospital.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Assess and act as you think the patient needs. Each assessment takes the time on its button.
Partway through you are asked to write what you think is happening. A debrief scores what you did.

why.question: Mr. Ferraro is drowsier, vomiting and his right pupil is larger. What is happening, and what do you do?

parts.label: What is happening
parts.criteria: A head strike on an oral anticoagulant, then a drop in GCS, vomiting and pupil inequality, points to an intracranial bleed; the risk factors were the patient's (age, anticoagulant, urgency), the environment (wet floor) and the equipment (alarm off, walker out of reach).
parts.modelAnswer: He hit his head while on an anticoagulant, and now his GCS has dropped, he's vomiting and one pupil is bigger. That's a bleed until a CT says otherwise. The fall came from his own risks plus a wet floor, an alarm left off and a walker out of reach.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Provider now for an urgent CT; neuro checks continued; no sedative; the room made safe; hand off the anticoagulant and times.
parts.modelAnswer: Call the provider now for an urgent CT, keep doing neuro checks, give nothing sedating, fix the room, and hand off the anticoagulant and the times.

noProgress.rationale: A head strike on an anticoagulant with falling consciousness still without a CT an hour on is harm here.

unsafe.headline: A sedative after a head strike
unsafe.body: Sedation hides the signs you are watching for. After a head strike, especially on an anticoagulant, nothing sedating until the provider has assessed.

worsened.headline: Herniation
worsened.body: A 1-point drop in GCS, vomiting or a new pupil difference after a head strike on an anticoagulant needs the provider and a CT now.

wrongRoute.headline: Left for the day team
wrongRoute.body: An incident report is not escalation. Falling consciousness is called at once.

target.headline: Called in time
target.body: You checked before moving him, fixed the room, watched his neurology and called the drop within minutes. That is the expert path.

recovered.headline: CT, with delays
recovered.body: Check how long the drop in consciousness went before the call.

time_up.headline: No CT
time_up.body: A head strike on an anticoagulant with neurological change needs a CT urgently.

scoring.modelReasoning: An 81-year-old on an anticoagulant who hits his head is at high risk of a bleed, whatever he says. He is checked for injury before moving, the room's risk factors are fixed (alarm, walker, floor, call light), and neurological checks start. A 1-point drop in GCS with vomiting and a larger pupil means a possible intracranial bleed: the provider comes now for an urgent CT, and nothing sedating is given.
